Learned Helplessness. In the 1960s, Martin Seligman and Steven Maier conducted experiments that revealed something dark about what happens to organisms when they lose control. Dogs exposed to inescapable electric shocks later failed to escape shocks even when escape was suddenly possible. Instead, they remained passive, and this passivity persisted. Seligman termed the phenomenon learned helplessness, and it would reshape how we understand depression and resilience.

The experiment worked in two phases. In the first, dogs were divided into three groups. Some received shocks they could escape by pushing a panel; some received inescapable shocks; a control group received no shocks. In the second phase, all three groups were placed in a shuttle-box where they could escape shocks simply by jumping a barrier.

The results were stark. Dogs that had experienced inescapable shocks showed no escape attempts and passively endured the new shocks. The other two groups quickly learned to escape. Seligman proposed that the inescapable shocks had taught the dogs a lesson: their actions were futile. This produced a generalized expectancy of helplessness that persisted even in a new situation where escape was possible.

But learned helplessness was not inevitable. Dogs with some history of control, or prior success with escaping, showed resilience. Prior mastery conferred protection. Seligman extended the model to depression in humans. Loss, failure, and uncontrollability—when people perceive that their actions cannot change outcomes—can produce passivity, learned helplessness, and depressive symptoms. The work became central to cognitive models of depression and sparked research into optimism, resilience, and how the therapeutic restoration of agency could reverse these effects.
